Isidore too, in his book on the fathers of both Testaments, records that this same man "preached the gospel to the peoples of Spain and of the western regions, and poured the light of his preaching into the setting of the world"; and Freculph of Lisieux, following Isidore, records the same. The author of the chronicle that circulates under the name of Maximus, bishop of Saragossa, likewise asserts that James "was the first of all the apostles to preach on the western coasts." That he preached to the Britons is affirmed by the man who assumed the mask of Flavius Lucius Dexter, and that he preached to the Irish by Vincent of Beauvais.

The former, in his chronicle, at the year of Christ 41, says: "On his return James visited the Gauls, and the Britains, and the towns of the Veneti, where he preaches; and he returns to Jerusalem, to consult the blessed Virgin and Peter on matters of the gravest weight." The latter, in his Speculum Historiale — cited also at the Council of Basel by Alfonso García de Santa María, envoy of the king of Castile — writes as follows: "While the apostles were setting out for the various regions of the world, James, by the will of God, landed on the coasts of Ireland and fearlessly preached the word of God, where he is said to have chosen seven disciples — namely Torquatus, Secundus, Indaletius, Tisephons, Euphrasius, Caecilius, and Hesychius — so that through their fellowship he might root out the tares and entrust the seeds of the word of God to the dry and long-barren earth. And when his last day drew near, he proceeded with them to Jerusalem, and there underwent martyrdom."

Others, however, show that James was killed by Herod before the apostles had been divided among the "various regions of the world" (as Vincent, following Turpin, puts it) — indeed, the very authors whom Vincent himself followed show as much.
